app.title: Still Out There
app.tagline: They stopped talking. They never left.
app.notNasa: A student project for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Not made or endorsed by NASA.
intro.moon: This is the Moon as it looks from Earth at this moment. Four machines from the Apollo years are still sitting on it. One of them still has a job.
intro.mars: This is Mars at this moment. The dark side is where it is night. Two rovers, a lander and a helicopter are resting in the dust.
intro.deep: These two machines are not on any world. They are drifting through space. Every distance on this line is calculated for this exact second.

about.title: Sources and method
about.lead: Every fact in every story comes from one of the pages below. A script refuses to build the site if a fact has no checked source. The live numbers are calculated, never guessed.
about.sorted: About locations: the challenge resource list puts Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer and Kepler under 'Mars'. None of them are at Mars, so every machine here is placed where it really is.
about.live.mars: Mars time uses NASA's Mars24 algorithm. Our code is tested against the worked examples NASA publishes.
about.live.moon: Sunlight on the Moon uses the open-source Astronomy Engine library to find where the Sun is in the Moon's sky.
about.live.deep: Spacecraft distances come from tables downloaded from NASA's JPL Horizons system.
story.eagle.why: I am Eagle. Well… the bottom half of Eagle. On 20 July 1969, I carried two astronauts down to the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon. People had never landed on another world before. My job was easy to say and hard to do: land softly, and keep two humans safe. Want to know my trick?
story.eagle.how: I was built in two parts, called stages. My bottom half held the landing rocket and its fuel: more than 8,000 kg of it. My top half was a small cabin with its own engine. Why two parts? Because flying home is easier when you leave the heavy, empty part behind. Can you guess which part was me?
story.eagle.found: Neil Armstrong stepped off my ladder first. The moonwalk lasted a little over two hours. The astronauts collected 21.55 kg of Moon rock and soil, and they set up experiments near me. One is a special mirror for lasers, and scientists still use it today. But the visit was short. Do you know how short?
story.eagle.lastDay: After 21 hours and 36 minutes on the Moon, my top half fired its engine. I was the launch pad. It flew away with the astronauts, and I stayed. I have not moved since 21 July 1969. I am not sad about it. Staying behind was always the plan. So, who will land next?
story.eagle.carriesOn: New landers are being built right now. NASA's Artemis program is working with companies on 'human landing systems'. That is the grown-up name for Moon landers like me. NASA says its first Artemis landing with astronauts is planned for 2028. When they arrive, I will be right here, exactly where I landed.
story.lrv.why: Vroom! Okay, there is no sound on the Moon. I am a Moon car, and my real name is Lunar Roving Vehicle. Apollo 15 brought me to the Moon on 30 July 1971, next to a long valley called Hadley Rille. Before me, astronauts could only walk. With me, they could go exploring. How far? Hold on tight.
story.lrv.how: For the trip, I was folded up and hung on the side of the lander. My wheels had no rubber. Each tire was woven from thin steel wire, with strips of titanium metal for grip. Every wheel had its own electric motor, and two batteries gave the power. A folding car with wire wheels. Cool, right?
story.lrv.found: On Apollo 15, astronauts drove me 27.8 km and collected 77.31 kg of rocks and soil. Two more Moon cars followed on Apollo 16 and Apollo 17. The Apollo 17 car drove the farthest: 35.9 km in total, and up to 7.6 km away from its lander. Would you drive that far from your only ride home?
story.lrv.lastDay: My batteries could not be charged again. They were made for one visit only. My last drive on Apollo 15 was on 2 August 1971. Then the astronauts flew home, and I stayed on the Moon. I was built for three days of adventure, and I gave my very best. So who will drive on the Moon next?
story.lrv.carriesOn: NASA's Artemis program plans to send astronauts on harder and harder missions, to explore more of the Moon. Exploring more means going farther than legs can carry you. I showed that wheels work up here, even wheels made of wire. I hope the next Moon car has a softer seat than mine.
story.retro.why: Hello! I am a retroreflector. That is a special mirror that sends light straight back to where it came from. Astronauts left three of us on the Moon, on Apollo 11, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15. I am the Apollo 14 one. We sat next to science stations, like the one on Apollo 12 that felt the ground shake. Those are off now. But me? Keep reading.
story.retro.how: I am made of 100 little glass prisms called corner cubes. My big sibling from Apollo 15 has 300. And here is the best part: I need no power at all. No battery, no solar panel, nothing to break. Telescopes on Earth fire a laser at me, I bounce the light back, and they time the trip. Simple, right?
story.retro.found: By timing the laser, scientists measure the distance to the Moon to within a few millimeters. That is how they learned the Moon is slowly moving away from Earth, by 3.8 cm every year. They also learned that the Moon's core is liquid. All of that from a mirror that just sits here! Guess when I stopped working?
story.retro.lastDay: Trick question. I never stopped! The science stations near us, called ALSEP, were switched off on 30 September 1977. But lasers still find me. A telescope in New Mexico, now part of a NASA network, fires at us several times a month. I am the Moon machine that still has a job.
story.retro.carriesOn: Right now, a laser beam from Earth could be on its way to me. I never know when, so I am always ready. Every bounce adds to a measurement that started in 1969. Other machines here have gone quiet. I just keep sending your light back home, one flash at a time.
story.surveyor3.why: Before people could land on the Moon, somebody had to check the ground. Is it safe? Would a lander sink? That somebody was me, and I am a robot. I launched on 17 April 1967 and flew to a huge dark plain called the Ocean of Storms. I had a camera and a little digging arm. My landing was… bumpy.
story.surveyor3.how: I did not land once. I landed three times! I bounced off the Moon twice, and the first bounce was 10 meters high. Then I finally sat still and got to work. People on Earth sent commands to my digging arm. I dug four trenches and pushed on the soil to test how strong it was.
story.surveyor3.found: I sent 6,326 TV pictures back to Earth. My digging and pushing showed what Moon soil is like up close, and how much weight it can hold. That mattered a lot. Two years later, astronauts would trust that same ground with their lives. And two of them would come to visit me. Yes, really!
story.surveyor3.lastDay: Night on the Moon lasts about two weeks. My last contact with Earth was on 4 May 1967, two days after the night began. After that, I was silent. I sat alone in the dust for two and a half years. Then, on 19 November 1969, something moved on the horizon. Can you guess what it was?
story.surveyor3.carriesOn: It was Apollo 12! It landed only 180 meters away. Astronauts Conrad and Bean walked over and took some of my parts back to Earth, including my camera and my scoop. Robots first, people second: it worked. NASA's Artemis program now plans to send astronauts to explore more of the Moon.
story.sojourner.why: Hi! I am Sojourner. I was the first rover ever sent to Mars. A rover is a robot on wheels. I am small: 10.6 kg, and only 30 cm tall. I rode inside a lander called Pathfinder. We left Earth on 4 December 1996 and reached Mars on 4 July 1997. Want to hear about our wild landing?
story.sojourner.how: We did not land gently. We bounced! Big airbags puffed up around the lander. We hit Mars and bounced about 15 times, as high as 15 meters, like a giant beach ball. When we stopped, the lander opened up. On our second day on Mars, I stood up and rolled down a ramp onto the red ground.
story.sojourner.found: I carried a tool that can tell what rocks are made of. Together, the lander and I did more than 15 tests on rocks and soil. I took 550 pictures, and the lander took more than 16,500. We saw rounded pebbles, the kind that running water makes. It was a clue: long ago, Mars was warmer and wetter.
story.sojourner.lastDay: On 27 September 1997, our last data reached Earth. Then the connection was lost, and nobody knows exactly why. I could not call home anymore. I was little, but I showed something big: a robot on wheels can explore another planet. Do you know who came rolling after me?
story.sojourner.carriesOn: After me came bigger rovers. Spirit and Opportunity landed in 2004. Perseverance landed in 2021, and it even brought a helicopter! Every one of them follows a path that began with my little wheels. Go and meet Opportunity next. That rover drove a very, very long way.
story.opportunity.why: I am Opportunity. My friends call me Oppy. I landed on Mars on 24 January 2004, on a flat plain called Meridiani Planum. My mission was to look for signs that Mars once had water. My builders hoped I would last 90 Martian days and drive 1,000 meters. I had other plans. Guess how long I kept going?
story.opportunity.how: I ran on sunshine. My solar panels turned sunlight into electricity, up to 140 watts in full Sun. Two batteries stored that energy for later. Six wheels carried me over sand and rock. Sunlight in, driving out. It is a simple deal, as long as the Sun can reach you. Remember that part. It matters later.
story.opportunity.found: I found tiny round stones, only a few millimeters wide. My team called them 'blueberries'. They are full of iron, and they formed inside rock that was soaked with water. I also found hematite, a mineral that forms in water. So Mars was wet, long ago! And I kept driving: 45.16 km. That is longer than a marathon.
story.opportunity.lastDay: In June 2018, a dust storm covered all of Mars. The sky went dark, and my solar panels could not make power. Earth last heard from me on 10 June 2018. My team sent more than a thousand commands to wake me up. They tried one last time on 12 February 2019. I rest in a place called Perseverance Valley.
story.opportunity.carriesOn: I was built for 90 days. I explored for more than 14 years. Today a newer rover is working on Mars. Its name is Perseverance, just like my valley, and it landed in 2021. My rocks showed that Mars once had water. Now others follow that clue. Not bad for a 90-day robot, right?
story.opportunity.sister: Spirit landed in January 2004 too, in a place called Gusev Crater, far away on the other side of Mars. She drove 7.7 km. In April 2009 her wheels broke through a thin crust into soft sand, and she could hardly move. Her last message came on 22 March 2010.
story.ingenuity.why: Wheee! I am Ingenuity, a little helicopter. I rode to Mars under the belly of a rover called Perseverance. We landed on 18 February 2021 in Jezero Crater. My mission was a test: can anything fly on Mars? Nobody had ever tried. The plan was no more than five short flights in 30 days. Only five? Ha!
story.ingenuity.how: Flying on Mars is hard. The air is only about 1% as thick as the air on Earth, so my blades have almost nothing to push on. My answer: spin fast! My two rotors, each 1.2 meters long, turn about 2,400 times a minute in opposite directions. And I am light, only 1.8 kg. Ready for takeoff?
story.ingenuity.found: On 19 April 2021, I lifted off, hovered 3 meters up, and landed. It took 39.1 seconds. It was the first powered, controlled flight on another planet! Under my solar panel I carry a tiny piece of cloth from the Wright brothers' first airplane. Then I kept going: 72 flights, 17 km, as high as 24 meters.
story.ingenuity.lastDay: Flight 72 was on 18 January 2024. I climbed to 12 meters and hovered. On the way down, about 1 meter above the ground, I lost contact with my rover. The sand below was smooth, and that made it hard for me to see how I was moving. Later, a photo showed the shadow of a broken rotor blade. I could not fly again.
story.ingenuity.carriesOn: I was planned for 30 days, and I flew for almost three years. Now a bigger flying robot is getting ready. Its name is Dragonfly. It will fly from place to place on Titan, a moon of Saturn. NASA says it will launch no earlier than July 2028 and arrive in late 2034. Happy flying, Dragonfly!
story.insight.why: I am InSight. Other robots look at the outside of Mars. I came to study the inside. I launched on 5 May 2018 and landed on 26 November 2018, on a flat, smooth plain called Elysium Planitia. I have no wheels. I sat still on purpose. Why? Because I was listening. Shh… did you feel that?
story.insight.how: My robot arm, 1.8 meters long, lifted a seismometer off my deck and set it on the ground. A seismometer feels tiny shakes in the ground. On Mars, those shakes are called marsquakes. The shaking travels through the planet's crust, mantle and core, and it changes on the way. Reading it is like seeing inside a planet.
story.insight.found: I felt 1,319 marsquakes! The biggest came on 4 May 2022. It was about magnitude 5, the largest quake ever detected on another planet. But not everything worked. My heat probe, 'the mole', was built to dig 5 meters down. The soil was too clumpy to grip, and it only reached about 40 cm. Science is like that sometimes.
story.insight.lastDay: Dust was my problem. Little by little, it covered my solar panels, and I made less and less power. My team had a clever idea: I sprinkled dirt on my own panels on windy days, and the wind swept some dust away. It helped for a while. Earth last heard from me on 15 December 2022.
story.insight.carriesOn: I am quiet now, but my marsquake recordings are not. Scientists keep studying them, and they still find surprises about what is inside Mars. And the mole that got stuck? NASA says its data will help future missions that dig. Nothing is wasted. Not even the 'oops'. What would you listen for on Mars?
story.pioneer10.why: Dear Earth, this is Pioneer 10. I left you on 2 March 1972. My job was to go where no machine had gone: past Mars, through the asteroid belt, and on to the giant planet Jupiter. I was built for a trip of 21 months. Nobody was sure a spacecraft could get through. I am writing to tell you: it can.
story.pioneer10.how: I have no solar panels. I carried my own power in devices called RTGs. They make electricity from the heat of a special radioactive fuel. At Jupiter they gave me about 140 watts for my radio and my 11 science instruments. But that power fades a little every year. Remember that for later.
story.pioneer10.found: I entered the asteroid belt on 15 July 1972 and came out safely in February 1973. I was the first! On 4 December 1973, I flew past Jupiter, 130,354 km from the giant planet, and took about 500 pictures. Then I kept going. In 1983, I crossed the orbit of Neptune. And I still did not stop.
story.pioneer10.lastDay: My power grew weaker every year. On 23 January 2003, I sent my last signal. I was 12.23 billion km from Earth, and the signal needed 11 hours and 20 minutes to arrive. You called me one more time, on 4 March 2006. I could not answer. I am not gone. I am only too quiet to hear.
story.pioneer10.carriesOn: I carry a small metal plaque. It shows a man and a woman, and where and when I came from. It is a postcard, in case anyone ever finds me. I am heading toward a red star called Aldebaran. I should pass it in about two million years. Until then, think of me sometimes. Love, Pioneer 10.
story.kepler.why: I am Kepler, a space telescope. I launched on 6 March 2009 with one big job: search for exoplanets. An exoplanet is a planet that circles another star, not our Sun. They are so far away that you cannot simply look and see them. So I had to be clever. How do you find a planet you cannot see?
story.kepler.how: I stared at stars. Lots of them. The plan was to watch about 100,000 stars and wait. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star gets a tiny bit dimmer. That is called a transit. To hold perfectly still, I used spinning wheels called reaction wheels. I needed three. I had four. Lucky, right?
story.kepler.found: I found more than 2,600 planets outside our solar system! Because of me, we know our galaxy has more planets than stars. In May 2013, my second wheel broke, and only two were left. My team did not give up. They invented a new mission called K2. They hoped for 10 rounds of watching the sky. I did 19.
story.kepler.lastDay: In the end, I ran out of fuel. Without fuel, I could not do science anymore. NASA retired me on 30 October 2018. On 15 November 2018, I received my final commands. My team called them my 'goodnight' commands. I am still out here, drifting in a safe orbit around the Sun. Goodnight is not goodbye.
story.kepler.carriesOn: Another planet hunter carries on. Its name is TESS, and it launched in April 2018. It searches around 200,000 of the brightest and nearest stars. So tonight, when you look up, remember: our galaxy has more planets than stars. I helped count them. Which star would you check first?
mythcard.lastwords.myth: Opportunity's last words were: "My battery is low and it's getting dark."
mythcard.lastwords.fact: Not quite. Rovers do not send sentences. They send numbers. Opportunity's last data showed that it was low on power as the dust storm closed in. A science reporter named Jacob Margolis turned those numbers into words, and wrote that the data 'basically' meant this. People shared it as if the rover had said it. It is still a beautiful line. Now you know who wrote it.
mythcard.bacteria.myth: Bacteria from Earth survived on Surveyor 3's camera for more than two years on the Moon.
mythcard.bacteria.fact: Probably not. When the camera came home, scientists did find a common bacterium on it. But a later review of how the camera was studied found a big problem: the people handling it wore short sleeves, so germs from their skin could have got onto it. The lead reviewer said the team 'only detected their own contamination'.
mythcard.flags.myth: The flags that the Apollo astronauts planted on the Moon have all fallen down by now.
mythcard.flags.fact: Most are still standing! In 2012, the camera team of NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter found flag shadows at every Apollo landing site except one: Apollo 11. Astronaut Buzz Aldrin reported that the Apollo 11 flag was blown over by the engine blast when Eagle's top half took off.
media.eagle.caption: Eagle on the Moon, 20 July 1969. Buzz Aldrin unloads science experiments from the descent stage, the part that is still there today. Neil Armstrong took the picture.
media.eagle.alt: The Apollo 11 lunar module standing on four legs on grey ground under a black sky. An astronaut works beside its gold-wrapped lower half.
media.lrv.caption: 31 July 1971. James Irwin works at the Lunar Roving Vehicle, with Mount Hadley behind. The shadow of the lander is in front. David Scott took the picture.
media.lrv.alt: An astronaut beside the Moon car with a dish antenna, a big rounded mountain behind, and a dark shadow across the front of the picture.
media.retro.caption: The real thing: the laser retroreflector that Apollo 14 astronauts set up on the Moon on 5 February 1971.
media.retro.alt: A flat box tilted toward the sky, its top covered with a grid of small round prisms, sitting in dusty ground marked with bootprints.
media.surveyor3.caption: Two spacecraft on the Moon. Pete Conrad examines Surveyor 3's TV camera before taking it off. Apollo 12's lander is on the horizon behind him.
media.surveyor3.alt: An astronaut in a white spacesuit stands next to the spidery robot lander Surveyor 3. Far behind, on the horizon, is the small shape of the Apollo 12 lander.
media.sojourner.caption: Sojourner on Mars, just after driving off the lander. The picture was taken by the lander's camera.
media.sojourner.alt: Black and white picture of the small six-wheeled rover with a flat solar panel on top, sitting on rocky ground next to the lander's ramp.
media.opportunity.caption: The last images Opportunity took. They are tiny, because they are the real thing. The faint dot near the middle of each is the Sun, almost hidden by the dust storm.
media.opportunity.alt: Two small, grainy grey squares side by side. Each has a very faint pale dot near its centre: the Sun seen through thick dust.
media.ingenuity.caption: After its 72nd flight, Ingenuity took this picture of its own shadow on the sand. The rotor blade on the right is damaged.
media.ingenuity.alt: Orange sandy ground photographed from just above it. A dark shadow of a rotor blade crosses the picture; part of the blade's tip is missing.
media.insight.caption: InSight's final selfie, taken 24 April 2022. Compare it with its first selfie in 2018: the solar panels are now covered in dust.
media.insight.alt: The InSight lander seen from above, made of several pictures stitched together. Its two round solar panels are coated in orange-brown dust.
media.pioneer10.caption: Pioneer 10 being readied at Cape Kennedy in 1972. This picture shows where the plaque is mounted on the spacecraft.
media.pioneer10.alt: The Pioneer 10 spacecraft in a workshop: a large round dish antenna on top of a body wrapped in silver and gold foil, with a technician nearby.
media.kepler.caption: Kepler in a clean room at Ball Aerospace in Boulder, Colorado, before launch.
media.kepler.alt: A tall spacecraft wrapped in shiny gold foil stands in a large white clean room, with people in white suits working at its base.
media.insight.audio.title: Hear the biggest marsquake
media.insight.audio.caption: This is the magnitude 5 marsquake of 4 May 2022, the largest quake ever detected on another planet. InSight's seismometer felt the ground shake, and NASA turned those vibrations into sound you can hear.
media.insight.audio.transcript: What you hear: near silence, then a deep rumble that grows quickly, peaks, and slowly fades away over about 20 seconds. These are ground vibrations, not sound travelling through the air.
media.ingenuity.audio.title: Hear me fly on Mars
media.ingenuity.audio.caption: Recorded by the microphone on Perseverance during my fourth flight, on 30 April 2021. It was the first time a spacecraft recorded the sound of another spacecraft on another planet. NASA made my 84-hertz blade hum louder so you can hear it.
media.ingenuity.audio.transcript: What you hear: a low rumble of Martian wind the whole time, with a faint, steady hum on top. The hum is my blades. It gets louder and softer as I fly away from the rover and come back.
laser.title: Fire the laser
laser.lead: Do what scientists still do. Send a pulse of laser light to the mirrors on the Moon, and time how long it takes to come back.
laser.travelling: The light is on its way…
laser.result: Round trip: {s} seconds. That is real time, not sped up. Right now the Moon is about {km} km away.
laser.note: Distance calculated for this moment with Astronomy Engine, from Earth's surface to the Moon's surface (approximate). Real observatories time the pulse to measure the distance to within a few millimeters.

rollcall.surveyor3: Surveyor 3. Ocean of Storms, on the Moon. Silent since 1967.
rollcall.eagle: Eagle. Sea of Tranquility. Left behind in 1969.
rollcall.lrv: Lunar Roving Vehicle. Hadley Rille. Parked since 1971.
rollcall.sojourner: Sojourner. Ares Vallis, on Mars. Silent since 1997.
rollcall.pioneer10: Pioneer 10. Leaving the solar system. Silent since 2003.
rollcall.kepler: Kepler. Drifting around the Sun. Silent since 2018.
rollcall.retro: Apollo 14 laser mirror. Fra Mauro. Still working.
rollcall.title: Roll call
rollcall.lead: Ten machines. One question: who is still out there? Each one answers in its own voice, in the order it went quiet.
rollcall.end: Nine are silent. One still answers every time a laser from Earth reaches it. All ten are still out there.
rollcall.pick: Choose any machine to hear its story.
rollcall.note: Voices are AI-generated (elevenlabs.io). Every place and year comes from the sourced facts in each story.
boot.line: Calculating where the Sun is right now
about.why.title: Why we built this
about.why: People have left machines all over the solar system, and most kids have never heard of them. Space history is usually told as finished events. We wanted to show that these machines are still out there, right now: the Sun still rises on them, and one of them is still part of an experiment that is running today.
real.english: Sources are quoted in English, as published.
note.opportunity: The pin and local time are for Opportunity's landing site. It drove 45 km and rests in Perseverance Valley, on the rim of Endeavour Crater; NASA has not published exact coordinates for that spot.
note.ingenuity: The pin shows the Perseverance landing site in Jezero Crater. Ingenuity rests at its final airfield, nicknamed 'Valinor Hills', in the same crater; NASA has not published exact coordinates for that spot.
story.music.title: Soft music made for this story. It plays quietly under the voice.
